Hi Javier,

I think the informational metadata footprint in Glue is intentional, and I
would be cautious about making Glue mirror HMS here.

GlueCatalog and Lake Formation have a different design principle from HMS.
For Glue, the catalog entry is primarily a control-plane/catalog
representation of the Iceberg table, while the Iceberg metadata remains the
source of truth. Lake Formation then defines the authorization boundary for
access to that catalog metadata and to the underlying data/iceberg metadata.

HMS serves a different purpose. It is also an interoperability surface for
Hive clients, which historically inspect HMS table parameters directly.
That is why Iceberg projects much more state into HMS, including table
properties and derived metadata such as schema, partition spec, sort order,
and snapshot information.

frequently.

requiring every update to rewrite the affected region immediately.

more time reading a few index files could still be a good trade-off, since
we can avoid going back to the base table entirely.

object-store reads, the reconciliation cost, or something else that makes
the latency difficult to bound even when the number of overlay files is
strictly limited.

Hi everyone,

I'd like the community's call on how REST servers should send residuals
while
clients migrate to the new expression syntax, and I'm proposing conformance
fixtures in apache/iceberg-verification to track that migration.

Background

The expressions spec (apache/iceberg#17138) changed the preferred predicate
form:

  before (deprecated):  {"type": "eq", "term": "id", "value": 5}
  after (preferred):    {"type": "eq", "left": {"type": "reference",
"name": "id"}, "right": 5}

It also adds "literals" objects and "apply". Java, Go and C++ still read
and write
only the deprecated predicate form (Go checked by running it; Java and C++
by
reading the source).

1. Residuals during the migration

The spec says services should omit residuals unless the client supports the
new
syntax, "for example, via client version". But the Java reference server
always
sends residuals, and there's no reliable way to detect support:
X-Client-Version
isn't in the REST spec, and Java sends its library version while iceberg-go
sends
the REST spec version. Options:

  a. Always omit residuals. Simple and correct, but clients re-evaluate the
full
     filter per task instead of the server's simplified residual.
  b. Clients declare support explicitly (an optional PlanTableScanRequest
field
     or a spec-defined header); servers send new-form residuals only to
them.
  c. Infer from client version. Unreliable, for the reason above.

I'd suggest (b), with readers in every implementation updated before any
writer
switches.

2. Conformance fixtures

Add read-conformance surfaces to apache/iceberg-verification for expression
JSON
(deprecated and preferred forms) and REST scan tasks. Implementations opt
in, and
forms they can't read yet show up as UNSUPPORTED, so the migration is
visible
across implementations. Does this fit the next phase of
apache/iceberg-verification#10? Happy to open the PRs.

Related spec-doc fixes, filed separately:
  - Drop {"type":"true"} from OpenAPI:
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/18351
  - Hex case for binary/fixed:
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/18352

Thanks,
Revanth

[Reopning voting after going through reviews from @adutra]

Hi all,

Following the discussion thread [1], I'd like to call a vote on
standardizing the client User-Agent format in the REST catalog spec.

What a +1 endorses:
- Clients identify themselves with the standard HTTP User-Agent header
  (RFC 7231): whitespace-separated product/version tokens, most specific
  first (engine, then any integration or connector, then the Iceberg
  library, then the runtime), with an optional parenthesized comment for
  extra context. Example:

    Spark/4.0.0 iceberg-spark/1.9.0 iceberg-java/1.9.0 (scala 2.13.16)

- When the header is sent, the Iceberg library token (iceberg-java,
  pyiceberg, iceberg-rust, iceberg-go) must be present.
- The header is advisory. Servers must not reject a request just because
  it is missing or malformed, and must not use it for authentication.
  Servers may refuse operations from client versions known to be unsafe.
  It is not a capability negotiation mechanism.

The spec change is in PR [2]. If the vote passes, the follow-ups are
conforming the client libraries (java, python, rust, go) to emit this
format.

[ ] +1 Adopt this User-Agent format in the REST spec
[ ] 0
[ ] -1 Do not adopt (please explain)

Thanks,
Rahul

Hi Manu,

Good question.

This is not for single-value lookups. `Table.Labels()` already covers that.
The metadata table is for consumers that work with metadata as Arrow.

The design is the same across clients, but PyIceberg is probably the
clearest example. In PyIceberg, inspect already returns PyArrow, so labels
fit naturally there. You can do something like
`pa.concat_tables([t.inspect.labels() for t in tables])` and then
filter/group across many tables for things like PII, ownership, or cost
attribution. There is no DESCRIBE-style surface in the client.

For Go/Rust/C++ the main benefit is consistency. iceberg-go already exposes
snapshots, history, manifests, etc. through InspectTable; labels can use
the same path instead of special-casing the nested map. I also plan to add
`iceberg inspect <table> labels` to the CLI.

One caveat: only REST catalogs return labels today, so this is empty
elsewhere, and for simple per-table access the typed accessor is enough.

That’s why I think this fits the client inspect APIs better than
Java/Spark, where the SQL surface already exists.

In v4, we introduced the notion of *tightness* in stats. Tightness

body:
I've been thinking through the patterns where per-column tightness would
matter.

   1.

   *Selectively marking variable-length columns tight*. I don't have a use
   case for this yet. A file-level flag can still mean every non-truncated
   column is tight.
   2.

   *Selectively re-tightening a few columns, for example after a column
   update*. Dan's point from the discussion applies here: a workload whose
   DVs invalidate stats will also invalidate new column stats. A table left in
   a state where only some stats are tight due to an update seems unlikely.
   3.

   *A DV writer that can write tight stats*. This is the pattern that
   matters to me. The writer repairs bounds while it deletes, and it can
   repair every column it tracks. We still need an explicit flag, because
   otherwise readers treat any attached DV as wide and ignore the repaired
   bounds. One file-level flag covers this.
   4.

   *A command that restores tight stats when the DV writer cannot.* This is
   worth supporting when deletes are infrequent: write the DVs, analyze once,
   and use the tight bounds until the next DV. If we frequently write DV's
   then we are in the same bad situation as #2. Either way the restore is
   all-or-nothing. I thought for a bit that there could be a command that only
   restores stats for select columns, this could make sense with column update
   files but also feels like unecessary complexity.

Patterns 3 and 4 are the realistic ones, and both only need the file-wide
flag. So I'm kind of leaning in that direction now.

I think issue underpins that there's a "split-brain" issue with both HMS
and Glue, since they both have their own metadata and also rely on the
Iceberg metadata.

In both HMS and Glue, the catalog implementations reflect some (but not
all) information in their managed metadata.  For example, HMS stores the
schema and properties, but not the partitioning or sort order.  Glue stores
the schema, but not other properties, partitioning, or sort order.  In both
cases, the schema may not be converted/reflected perfectly (time/UUID/ect).

What's worse is that in both HMS and Glue, if you use tools that work
natively with the catalog APIs (e.g. the AWS console or SDK), you can
update the representation so that it isn't consistent with the underlying
Iceberg table metadata.

I don't know how much you can trust that the metadata is being kept in sync
and would definitely not rely on it for security or governance purposes.

Hi Javier,

I think the informational metadata footprint in Glue is intentional, and I would be cautious about making Glue mirror HMS here.

GlueCatalog and Lake Formation have a different design principle from HMS. For Glue, the catalog entry is primarily a control-plane/catalog representation of the Iceberg table, while the Iceberg metadata remains the source of truth. Lake Formation then defines the authorization boundary for access to that catalog metadata and to the underlying data/iceberg metadata.

HMS serves a different purpose. It is also an interoperability surface for Hive clients, which historically inspect HMS table parameters directly. That is why Iceberg projects much more state into HMS, including table properties and derived metadata such as schema, partition spec, sort order, and snapshot information.

Best,

Shawn

Hi all, a question about GlueCatalog and what it writes to the Glue table on commit.

GlueTableOperations.prepareProperties<https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/d008ad230bed30383a667af8151573e48de7624c/aws/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/aws/glue/GlueTableOperations.java#L291-L301> sets only table_type, metadata_location and previous_metadata_locationin the Glue table Parameters. It carries over whatever parameters the Glue table already had, but never copies TableMetadata.properties().

The Hive catalog works differently. HMSTablePropertyHelper.updateHmsTableForIcebergTable<https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/d008ad230bed30383a667af8151573e48de7624c/hive-metastore/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/hive/HMSTablePropertyHelper.java#L78-L130> pushes all Iceberg table properties into HMS params, plus the current snapshot summary, schema, partition spec and sort order, all capped by iceberg.hive.table-property-max-size (https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/d008ad230bed30383a667af8151573e48de7624c/hive-metastore/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/hive/HiveOperationsBase.java#L53). So the same table shows a lot more metadata through HMS than through Glue.

Questions:

  1.  Is the minimal Glue footprint intentional? The javadoc says Glue info is "informational only" and metadata_location is the source of truth. Or has nobody needed more yet?
  2.  Would the community accept a change that mirrors the Hive behavior for Glue? That would mean syncing table properties (and maybe the snapshot summary/schema/spec) into Glue Parameters, with a size cap and an opt-in flag. Open design questions would be Glue's parameter size limits, removing keys that were deleted in Iceberg, and protecting reserved keys.

Our use case: tools that only read the Glue catalog (governance, discovery, Lake Formation-based tooling) can't see Iceberg table properties without opening the metadata JSON.

+1 on the file-wide flag.

to two parts.

The first is file-level and changes over time. A DV added later deletes
some rows, and the accuracy of the original bounds are no longer
guaranteed. The new file wide flag can help record the change.

The second is column-level and static. Variable-length columns like String
and Binary can have truncated bounds, so we cannot make them reliably
tight, and we don't have a use case that needs their tightness today.
That's a property of the column type in the schema, so it doesn't need
additional metadata for recording.

So moving the tightness boolean from per-column to per-entry (tracked_file
in v4) simplifies the bookkeeping for writers without giving up anything we
care about.

One note on upgrading the existing tables to v4. Since we want that to stay
a lightweight metadata operation with no manifest rewrite, tightness is
simply undefined for existing entries. Today the merge-on-read table does
not have tight bounds. Once position deletes and DVs are rewritten to be
colocated with the data file in a single tracked-file entry, tightness
becomes a well-defined property of that entry, and a writer at that point
can set the flag accordingly.

DECIMAL(25. 0) without rewriting data files. Existing Parquet files keep
storing the column as int32 with DECIMAL(8. 0) and readers must read them
as DECIMAL(25, 0).

The spec addresses reading narrower types in the context of schema
evolution. However, schema evolution can potentially leave no markers in
the metadata, so readers must be prepared to read narrower types than the
type specified in the schema. We have come across systems which do not read
all possible allowed types for columns but instead check for an exact type
match.

*Proposed Change*
PR: https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18404

Add one sentence to Schema Evolution, immediately after the table of valid
type promotions:

*"Readers must accept a data file column whose type is either the field's
type or a type that can be promoted to the field's type according to the
valid type promotions for the table's format version, regardless of whether
the field's type was evolved."*

Please let me know what you think. Feedback is welcome here or on the PR.

Thank you
Sandeep Gottimukkala

Thanks, everyone, for the input. Adding a none value works for me, as it
lets clients explicitly indicate that they do not need delegated access.

I'm fine with leaving the server's behavior unspecified for different
combinations of requested mechanisms, as long as failing the request is
also an option. My main concern is the case where a client
requests mechanism A (e.g., credential vending) but the server returns
mechanism B, like remote signing.

Here are a few scenarios:

   1. The client requests mechanism A, and the server provides A.
   2. The client requests mechanisms A and B, and the server provides A
   and/or B.
   3. The client sends none, and the server provides no delegated access.
   4. The client requests mechanism A, but the server cannot provide A and
   fails the request.

I think scenario 4 is both acceptable and expected.

Returning to Youngrae's original question, I suggest updating the wording
in the spec to:

Optional signal to the server that the client supports delegated access via
a comma-separated list of access mechanisms. The server may choose to
supply access via any or none of the requested mechanisms, or fail the
request.

body:
Hi all,

I'm Nevin. I'm building a governed table encryption feature based on
Apache Gravitino. I've been following the encryption-over-REST work
and would love to help move it forward, whether through reviews,
implementation, tests, or a short write-up of the options.

Reading the three PRs [1][2][3], the #17155 design doc [4] and
the earlier dev@ thread [5], I think the discussion comes down to two
design questions the spec hasn't settled yet:

1. May a client get storage and KMS credentials from different
sources (e.g. vended storage, its own KMS)?
See [4], [5], the review on [1], and [3].

2. Should naming the KMS be separate from supplying KMS credentials
(e.g. the catalog names it, the client uses its own credentials)?
See [1] and [2].

My current leaning is toward landing [1] first, narrowed as its
review proposed:

- This is the simple case: the client uses its own credentials for
both storage and KMS.
- The catalog passes KMS configuration (which KMS, e.g.
encryption.kms-type) as ordinary catalog properties, and each
table carries its encryption.key-id. These are pointers, not
credentials; they grant nothing.
- The REST client builds its KMS client from catalog and client
properties, as the Hive catalog client does today, and calls
the KMS with whatever credentials its environment provides.
- No new REST endpoints, fields or credential types. A source-
compatibility question about the protected newTableOps hooks was
raised on [1] and is still open.

On the mixed case from question 1, vended storage credentials with
the client's own KMS credentials ("hybrid" in [3]): it has real
value, as argued on [1], but needs more design, such as how a client
opts in and whether it fits [4]. I'm not opposed, and an explicit
opt-in flag as in [3] seems fine to me. Either way, I'd suggest the
simple case not wait on it.

I see a few benefits:

- Safe: the catalog needs neither key material nor KMS credentials;
key access stays with the client's own identity.
- Deployers: keys stay governed by their existing IAM.
- Catalog implementers: nothing to build beyond storing and
returning properties; no per-cloud KMS credential minting.
- Engines: the same encryption path as the Hive catalog.
- A flexible starting point: KMS credential vending [2] and other
access-delegation modes can be added later as opt-ins without
breaking it.

How this relates to the open proposals:

- [1] #13225: the simple case above; its review proposed this scope.
- [2] #17155: complementary. It covers the catalog vending KMS
credentials; the simple case covers clients using their own.
The two can coexist, and both use encryption.kms-type.
- [3] #18081: explores hybrid behind an opt-in flag; it can follow
once that design settles.
- [4] Design doc: consistent. The simple case vends nothing;
whether hybrid fits [4] is question 1.

I'd welcome any views on this and on the two questions above.
Thanks!

Warmly,
Nevin

[1] #13225 (Sreesh Maheshwar), Core: Support client-configured
encryption in RESTCatalog. The REST client builds a KMS client
from catalog and client properties.
https://www.google.com/url?q=https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/13225&source=gmail&ust=1791870345063000&sa=E
[2] #17155 (Adam Szita), Spec: REST KMS credential vending for table
encryption. Adds the kms-vended-credentials access-delegation
mode, encryption.kms-type as a catalog property, and
key-management-credentials keyed by KMS key ID.
https://www.google.com/url?q=https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17155&source=gmail&ust=1791870345063000&sa=E
[3] #18081 (Prashant Singh, draft), Core: [Demonstration only]
handle hybrid mode encryption with REST Catalog. Catalog-vended
storage credentials with the client's own KMS credentials,
behind an opt-in flag.
https://www.google.com/url?q=https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18081&source=gmail&ust=1791870345063000&sa=E
[4] "KMS credential vending for Iceberg table encryption" (Adam
Szita), design doc for #17155. Says a client must not be
required to combine delegated storage credentials with
client-local/static KMS credentials; a comment adds that they
"need to be vended either together or not at all".
https://www.google.com/url?q=https://docs.google.com/document/d/1VSewbVmjukU5eTiZruCJVmUZcRZvcAsd4JOeC6Lt3fo&source=gmail&ust=1791870345063000&sa=E
[5] dev@ thread, "[DISCUSS] REST Catalog: Credential management for
KMS/Vault and Table level Encryption" (Prashant Singh, May to
July 2026). The discussion that led to [4] and #17155.
https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.mail-archive.com/[email removed]/msg13452.html&source=gmail&ust=1791870345063000&sa=E

body:
Hi everyone,

I'd like to start a vote on adding the file data type to the v4 table spec,
as proposed in this PR:

https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17918

The spec change does the following:

New file type: a range of bytes stored either inline or as a reference to
an external file. Its value semantics follow the FILE logical type in the
Parquet spec.

Fixed, implicit sub-fields: uri, offset, size, content_type, checksum and
inline. They don't appear in the schema and can't be added, removed,
reordered or promoted. Their field IDs are offsets +1 to +6 from the file
field's ID, so adding a file field moves last-column-id forward by 7.

URIs: a uri can be absolute or relative. Relative URIs resolve against the
table location.

Stats: each sub-field gets its own field stats. Writers should produce
stats for uri, content_type and inline.

Restrictions:
- Equality, ordering and hashing aren't defined for file values.
- A file column can't be an identifier field or a source for partition or
sort transforms.
- A file column must default to null.
- A file isn't interchangeable with a struct that has the same sub-fields,
and can't be promoted from one.
- A uri doesn't guarantee the referenced file exists.

Format mappings:
- Parquet: map with the FILE logical type.
- Avro: record.
- ORC: struct with iceberg.struct-type=FILE.

JSON schema serialization: "file".

FILE type is v4 only. Writing file into a v3 or earlier schema is invalid.

Please vote in the next 72 hours.

[ ] +1 Add the File type to the v4 spec
[ ] +0
[ ] -1 I have concerns because...

Thanks,
Talat on behalf of FILE type working group

Hi Hongyue,

I'll quickly explain our use case here, but if you want an in-depth discussion of why we actually need this, look (and comment) here: https://lists.apache.org/thread.html/owfk09ll0n1crtfbl8jnyzmg8tm1dbrg.

Basically, with each append, we stuff our proprietary index into a statistics puffin file. Since there is currently no way to do manifests on these files, we have to read everything from the last snapshot's index, append new data, and write it into the new snapshot's puffin file. If another transaction won over our transaction, we need to re-read the new index state and write a brand new puffin file.

The SnapshotAncestryValidator can indeed cover the validation part, but as far as I understand, it can't encapsulate the retry logic of writing a new statistics file. We can start the transaction from the beginning, but with a custom PendingUpdate we can reduce the re-try scope to just the puffin file while keeping the data files valid. We will probably have some other types of updates too because we abuse the table properties for some global info.

At the end of the day, this is a philosophical discussion rather than a technical one. Opening this up will allow people to build on top of Iceberg easier, but it can also create incompatibilities between people's data, which is something that Iceberg became popular for. Some of these things would hopefully be merged upstream at some point though so it can really go both ways.

Cheers,
Filip

I had a longer discussion with Ryan and Russell at ApacheCon, and we
explored two main changes to the current spec:

   1. Store Region file *boundaries as top-level fields* in the tracking
   file schema instead of column stats. We still need to decide whether to
   reserve new field IDs or reuse existing field IDs, like the partition field
   IDs. Currently this former one is documented in the PR.
   2. *Store the actual Extract schema* directly in the index metadata
   instead of deriving it from `identity`, `materialized`, and
   `non-materialized` fields. This makes the index self-contained, at the cost
   of maintaining historical schemas and schema evolution rules. This also
   makes Derived Column support mandatory for indexes. See:
   https://docs.google.com/document/d/1u93kyIrTc8bt9VSTB4O0GM9S7zuXekqixJR6Id2FZC4

Please take a look and let me know what you think.

Peter

Hi, everyone -

We reached consensus on having a file-level tightness flag. Thanks to all
who contributed to the discussion. We think there is room for
further improvement. The notion of stats tightness currently only covers
the upper and lower bounds of the column. We propose expanding it to cover
null/NaN/value counts also. This would improve the coverage of
metadata-only query optimizations.

e.g. `SELECT count(1) from table where my_col is NULL` can be answered from
the metadata if we know that the stats are fully tight. As per the current
v4 spec  we can't do that because the tightness only covers the bounds
(except for the narrow cases where there are no nulls or all nulls, which
you can infer by comparing the null count to the value count).

We should also rename the field from `tight_bounds` to `tight_stats` to
accurately represent the semantics. Please let me know what you think. I
have added this as an agenda item to Monday's v4 Adaptive Metadata Tree
sync.

Hi everyone,

I opened a PR to add a standard HyperLogLog (HLL) blob type to the Puffin
spec and would like to hear your thoughts before it moves forward.

PR: https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18513
Issue: https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/18516

*Motivation*
Puffin currently defines only one blob type for NDV statistics,
apache-datasketches-theta-v1. In some workloads, Theta sketch computation
is slow. In Trino, it causes a 10-20% slowdown on inserts. Trino is
considering an HLL option (https://github.com/trinodb/trino/pull/31173).
Since the spec has no standard HLL type, that PR has to store the sketch as
an engine-specific blob type. That means other engines can’t read it.

*Proposal*
Add a new blob type, apache-datasketches-hll-v1:

   - It holds a serialized “compact” Apache DataSketches HLL sketch.
   - The sketch is built with the default seed. Individual distinct values
   are fed to it using Iceberg’s single-value serialization, the same as for
   the Theta type.
   - The blob metadata may include an ndv property, defined the same way as
   for the Theta type.

Feedback on the PR or in this thread is welcome.

Thanks,
Yuya

body:
Hi everyone,

I’d like to bring up a topic currently being discussed in PR
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18338 to the dev list to get broader
community input.

*Background*
As a quick refresher, the PR addresses a *silent correctness bug* regarding
equality delete files. Currently, when equality delete files are written
with the full row schema, columns outside the equality key might carry null
or sentinel values. The ManifestReader has been treating these non-key
column stats as reliable for metrics pruning. Consequently, certain
predicates (like col IS NOT NULL) can incorrectly skip valid delete
manifest entries, leaving rows in the query result that should have been
deleted (first observed in Trino
https://github.com/trinodb/trino/issues/31399).

*Discussion*

The open question (relevant for v2, v3, v4 format tables) I'm bringing up
is whether there are good reasons to keep on reading statistics for
non-equality ID columns from the equality delete files.

Additional note:
Filtering out stats when reading equality deletes is changing what
DeleteFile.lowerBounds()/valueCounts()/nullValueCounts() return, not just
how they're used for predicate matching.

Because this touches on core read-path behavior and how engines interpret
delete manifest stats, I think it would be valuable to get more eyes on
this and establish a consensus on the best path forward.

*Additional context*

https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#equality-delete-files

Equality delete files identify deleted rows in a collection of data files
by one or more column values, and may optionally contain additional columns
of the deleted row

Let me know your thoughts!

Thank you,

Marius Grama.

meta.subject: [DISCUSS] Handling of non-key column stats for equality delete files (PR #18338)

title: [DISCUSS] Handling of non-key column stats for equality delete files (PR #18338)

body:
The column stats are indeed collected by Flink in non-upsert mode. (In that
mode the equality delete row schema is the full table schema, and the
delete writer uses the table's metrics config. So non-key columns get
value/null counts and lower/upper bounds.)

If equality deletes were going to stay with us long term, I'd suggest
changing the spec to say: "Stats for columns not in equality_ids should not
be stored for equality delete files."

Since, equality deletes are being phased out, and v4 already forbids them.
Existing tables still carry these stats, so the practical fix is to ignore
them. I see two options:

   1. Drop the non-key stats when the manifests are read. This is a
   localized change in core. The non-key stats would no longer appear in
   metadata tables and would be permanently removed when manifests are
   rewritten. Since nothing legitimately uses them, that's harmless, and
   arguably a cleanup.
   2. Ignore them where they are used for filtering. This is what this PR
   does, in InclusiveMetricsEvaluator and StrictMetricsEvaluator. Stored
   metadata stays untouched, but the public evaluators now treat equality
   delete files differently.

My preference would be 1, but I would like to hear what others think, or I
miss some other uses of these stats.

Thanks,
Peter

body:
Hi all,

The spec allows NaN, Infinity and -Infinity as float and double values [1],
and doesn't restrict them as defaults [2]. But JSON single-value
serialization says float and double are a "JSON number" [3], and JSON
numbers can't be NaN or Infinity (RFC 8259, section 6). The same applies to
the REST spec, where FloatTypeValue and DoubleTypeValue are type: number
[4]. So there is no valid way to write, for example, initial-default =
+Infinity.

Today each client works around this differently:

- Java writes the strings "NaN", "Infinity" and "-Infinity". This comes
from Jackson's default, not from an explicit choice [5]. Java's own reader
then rejects these strings [6], so Java can't read back what it writes.
- iceberg-rust, PyIceberg and iceberg-cpp write null, so the value is
silently lost.
- iceberg-go refuses to write them.

Two questions:

1. Should the spec define how non-finite float and double values are
 serialized in JSON? I think it has to, so clients stop diverging.

2. If so, should we standardize what Java already writes, i.e. the exact,
 case-sensitive strings "NaN", "Infinity" and "-Infinity", with finite
values staying JSON numbers? That would mean updating Appendix D and the
two OpenAPI value types. Java would only need a reader fix, and the other
clients would align. The alternative is to say non-finite values must not
be written to JSON, in which case writers error, Java included.

Whichever we pick, I'd like it written down in the spec or as conformance
fixtures in iceberg-verification [7], so clients can check against it
instead of against each other.

Thanks,
Andrei

Hi, everyone -

Following the discussion on v4 stats tightness [1], I'd like to call a vote
on the spec change that replaces the per-column `tight_bounds` field with a
single file-level `tight_stats` flag.

Summary of the change:

   - Stats tightness is tracked once per file with a `tight_stats` flag on
   the tracked file instead of a `tight_bounds` field on every column's
   stats struct.
   - The tightness flag covers all statistics (bounds and null, NaN, and
   value counts), not just bounds, so metadata-only queries can trust the
   counts as well.
   - When the `tight_stats` flag is absent, readers must assume stats are
   not tight.
   - A deletion vector no longer implicitly makes stats wide; `tight_stats`
   is the authoritative indicator, and engines are allowed to retighten
   stats without rewriting data files.

References:

1. Discussion thread:
https://lists.apache.org/thread.html/tv7bvqctdfh5qng1sx5rp8r4r00nsv60
2. Design options doc:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/13DbwnwKQXjvY3vRcFJo-qVAQWk-GB4zLzzYmFdPntZg/

3. Spec PR: https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18585

[ ] +0
[ ] -1 Do not adopt, with reason

body:
I don't think that we are trying to solve the problem of generated columns
right now. I think that should be part of the schema so it is separate from
this work.

You might be suggesting that we use generated columns to store stats
instead of the current proposal. I don't think that is a good idea because
it adds extra fields to the schema with different behavior that breaks
assumptions for schemas.

For instance, stats-only fields are not fields in the schema and should not
be displayed as part of the table schema. Generated columns are part of
table data, which is why they belong in the schema. If we add stats-only
fields to the schema, then anyone consuming the schema needs to know what
to filter out before passing it along.

Similarly, schema fields have specific types that change only when a user
modifies them. Stats fields are derived and can change when schema changes
affect them, so we would not be able to produce all field types without
binding the schema to a subset of itself.

This would also complicate composition. Right now, stats-only fields are
not nested within the schema, they are independent. If we were allowing a
field to be a stat-only field then we have to come up with rules around
where they can be used (not in map keys?) and then check those rules. How
would you handle a struct with only one field that is a stats-only field
that is not actually present in the schema?

The proposal is much simpler because we don't need to worry about many of
these concerns.

Ryan

Hi all,

As discussed at the last Vector sync, I wrote some code and ran benchmarks
to measure how well Parquet handles embeddings stored as FLOAT and as
FLOAT16.

*ALP*: Parquet Java doesn't support ALP yet, so I prototyped it. It doesn't
compress these FLOAT16 embeddings well:

   - Plain ALP needs 36.5 bits/value even with zstd, which is more than raw
   float32.
   - ALP_rd + zstd needs 17.9 bits/value, 18% more than dictionary encoding
   (15.1).
   - Dictionary encoding needs 15.1 bits/value even without zstd: the
   embeddings have only ~24k distinct values, so every value becomes a 15-bit
   id.

*I have ruled out using ALP.*

*Read/write/heap*: Java has no native float16 type yet (
https://openjdk.org/jeps/508), so I expect Java users to store float16
values in shorts for now. The benchmark therefore uses float[] and short[]
as the in-memory embeddings.

Optimizations I made for both FLOAT and FLOAT16:

   - FLOAT16 values are decoded straight from the page, without allocating
   a Binary per value
   - Bulk reads of float/float16 lists, with faster PLAIN,
   BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT and dictionary decoding
   - Fixed-size lists: repetition/definition levels are derived instead of
   decoded
   - About 20% faster zstd page decompression
   - Column/size statistics turned off for columns nested in lists/maps,
   which Iceberg doesn't use anyway

Results on my MacBook Pro (M4 Pro, JDK 21), with 100,000 embeddings of
2,560 dimensions in local files:

   - *Smallest*: FLOAT16 + BSS + zstd is 10% smaller than FLOAT + DICT +
   zstd (415 vs 459 MiB), and also reads 22% faster (284 vs 362 ms).
   - *Fastest reads*: FLOAT16 + PLAIN + uncompressed reads 26% faster than
   FLOAT + PLAIN + uncompressed (134 vs 180 ms), at half the file size. On
   blob storage the extra transfer would increase the gap even more.
   - *Overall*: the best FLOAT setup is DICT + uncompressed, and the best
   FLOAT16 setup is PLAIN + uncompressed. They have similar sizes (459 vs 489
   MiB), but FLOAT16 reads 57% faster (134 vs 312 ms), writes 55% faster, and
   uses half the heap.

*I clearly see a lot to gain from Parquet's FLOAT16 type.*

body:
Hi all,

The review of #18003 asked to settle the direction for CDC (upsert and
delete) writes in the Kafka Connect sink on this list. Here is the proposal.

Background
- #14797 added a delta writer to the sink but was not merged, mainly
because equality deletes committed by a streaming sink slow down every
reader until compaction runs. v4 now forbids writing new equality deletes
(#17783).
- Flink converts equality deletes after they are committed.
ConvertEqualityDeletes (#15996, #17142) is a maintenance task that keeps a
primary key index in Flink state and converts the equality deletes of a
staging branch, or of the write branch in place, into deletion vectors.

Proposal
The sink's coordinator sees every file of a commit before committing it. It
resolves the batch's equality deletes against the base snapshot, writes
deletion vectors (merged with each data file's existing DV or v2 position
deletes), and commits the data files and the DVs in one RowDelta. The
equality delete files are never committed, not even as a fallback.

- Lookup: a stateless scan. Candidate files are pruned by the delete's
partition and the deleted keys, and only the key columns and _pos are read.
The lookup is behind an interface, so an index (#16961) can replace the
scan later.
- Concurrency: the RowDelta validates from the base snapshot, with the
deleted keys as the conflict filter, and checks that the data files the DVs
point to still exist, which catches a concurrent compaction. On a conflict,
the coordinator converts again against the new snapshot, and fails the
commit if conflicts keep coming.
- Series: part 1 is the converter (#18003, in review), part 2 calls it from
the coordinator and adds a benchmark, part 3 adds the delta writer, part 4
adds integration tests.

Why before the commit, without state
- Kafka Connect has no keyed state or checkpoints to keep an index in, and
a sink writing to many tables would need an index per table. The same
memory concern came up for Flink's dynamic sink in #17142.
- Readers never see equality deletes, and clients that cannot apply them
can still read the table.

Cost
The write side pays: every commit reads the key columns of the candidate
files, so the cost follows the number of files that can hold the deleted
keys. The expensive cases are keys that file bounds cannot prune (such as
random UUIDs), upsert mode, where every insert also deletes its key,
bucketed tables, where planning currently runs once per partition group,
and conflicts, which repeat the conversion. All of it runs on the
coordinator. Part 2 will benchmark the conversion time against the commit
interval and compare it with reads over accumulated equality deletes (plan
in the PR description). Past that envelope the conversion still runs, so
the cost shows up as commit latency rather than as equality deletes in the
table.

Format versions
- v3: deletion vectors let writers move off equality deletes before their
tables move to v4. Flink's converter also targets v3.
- v4: new DVs must be colocated with their data files, so v4 support comes
once the converter writes colocated DVs.
- v2: there are no deletion vectors, so CDC writes would not be supported
on v2 tables.

Questions
1. Is converting in the sink's commit path, before the commit and without
state, the right direction for Kafka Connect, alongside Flink's post-commit
conversion?
2. Is it acceptable that CDC writes require v3 or later, and that going
past the envelope costs commit latency instead of falling back to equality
deletes?
3. Should the deleted keys come from the identifier fields for now, and
from the primary key in the v4 constraints proposal (#17822) once it lands?

Links
- #18003: https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18003
- Benchmark envelope discussion:
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18003#discussion_r4374820473
- #14797: https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/14797
- #15996 and #17142 (Flink ConvertEqualityDeletes):
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/15996,
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17142
- Earlier thread on Flink's conversion:
https://lists.apache.org/thread/gldqrycmo24r0vo77wzcj9s9b04rtvy7
- #17783: https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17783
- #17822: https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17822

Hi all,

I'd like to pick up this thread with a report from an implementation.

Over the past months I built a proof of concept of multi-table,
multi-statement transactions in Apache Polaris: BEGIN/COMMIT across tables,
READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ, a read point that can be shared across
engines, and fan-out, where independent jobs each write part of one
transaction. It works with Spark, and with Trino for reads.

The work here helped shape it. Thanks to Maninderjit Singh and Jagdeep
Sidhu for the proposal and its two options, to Dmitri Bourlatchkov for the
discussion on how much of the ordering clients should see, and to Eduard
Tudenhöfner and Jack Ye for the earlier work in #6948 and #10617. Thanks
also to the people who discussed it with me at Lakehouse Day in Glasgow;
those conversations changed the design.

What surprised me most was how much of this Iceberg already supports.
Writes are staged on ordinary table branches and published with the
existing multi-table commit, using ref requirements. Engines use their
normal write paths, and the table format is unchanged. The only place it
touches a standard REST endpoint is one optional loadTable parameter for
the read point, which could equally live in a Polaris endpoint. Most of the
remaining work is in the catalog implementation.

The design doc covers the semantics and the Polaris API:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ew2dOI_BHQFP1C8Q46Y_m_AvNNH4rzzLKaSsB089GTU/edit?usp=sharing

Comments on the design are welcome directly in the doc. The Polaris
discussion is on dev@polaris (
https://lists.apache.org/thread/d5ft79ogcxx15ccr1n1bc0rvsl14tf6v), tracked
in https://github.com/apache/polaris/issues/5833. As suggested there, I'm
bringing the Iceberg-facing parts here. The PoC code will be published
after it is rebased onto current Polaris main.

Since most of this rests on primitives Iceberg already has, it raises a
question for this community: should the Iceberg REST spec define
transactions, or the primitives a catalog needs to offer them?

   - Consistent multi-table reads: an optional, catalog-defined opaque read
   point on loadTable.
   - Snapshot lifecycle coordination: letting snapshot expiry know which
   historical snapshots an active read point still references.
   - Requirement enforcement on unchanged tables: clarifying that a
   multi-table commit must enforce requirements on tables it doesn't update,
   which SERIALIZABLE isolation (not implemented yet) depends on.
   - Validated branch rebase: core support for re-applying a branch's
   changes onto a moved main with Iceberg's conflict validation, beyond
   today's fast-forward and cherry-pick; Write-Audit-Publish (WAP) workflows
   could also benefit.

Concretely, I'd appreciate views on two things:

   1. The framing above: minimal primitives in the Iceberg spec, with
   higher-level transaction semantics left to catalogs. Are these the right
   gaps to address?
   2. The read-point parameter: is an optional, catalog-defined parameter
   on loadTable something the REST spec should have, or should it stay in each
   catalog's own API?

This work explores transaction coordination inside Polaris, as an opt-in
extension built on Iceberg's existing primitives, to learn from real use.
As it uncovers missing lower-level primitives in the REST spec, like the
ones above, I'll bring each back here as its own small proposal; this
thread itself doesn't propose a spec change. The Polaris transaction
endpoints are Polaris's own extension and stay out of the spec.

If you see edge cases with this approach or a better way to achieve this, I
would love to hear your thoughts.

Thanks,
Qiegang

body:
Hi Andrei,

Thanks for the reply.

On whether the sink should do CDC at all: append plus MERGE works, and it
should remain available. But the history suggests the sink was meant to get
CDC back once the concerns about equality deletes were addressed:

- After the initial sink submission, Bryan opened #10842 [3]. Delta writer
support had been left out because of performance concerns over equality
deletes, and the issue says: "We should address those concerns and add back
the delta writer support, for features like change data capture and upsert
mode." It is still open.
- In [1], Ryan objected to the sink writing equality deletes, and Bryan
hoped the sink would get a solution like the one Flink was working on, for
streaming deletes without equality deletes.
- Users keep asking for it: #13986, #15046, #15342, #15351, #17542.

This proposal is meant to be that solution: the table never gets an
equality delete.

CDC would be opt-in, and append-only stays the default. Append plus MERGE
remains the better fit for two kinds of tables:
- Tables whose readers follow rows across updates by row ID. The sink
writes an update without reading the old row, so the new row cannot carry
the old row ID and gets a new one. The spec describes the same for equality
delete writers such as Flink's upsert, which don't read existing rows
either [4]. Spark's MERGE reads the old row and keeps its row ID.
- Tables where the conversion can't keep up with the commit interval. It
runs on the coordinator, and the part 2 benchmark will show where that
point is.

For other tables, the sink keeps the target table current at the commit
interval, without a separate MERGE job per table.

On repartitioning, which Ryan named as the main challenge for writing DVs
from Kafka Connect [2]: for CDC topics, Kafka already does it. Debezium
uses the primary key as the message key, Kafka's default partitioner sends
equal keys to the same partition, and Kafka Connect assigns each partition
to one task. So within a commit, all changes to a row reach the same task,
and the task resolves repeated changes itself. Rows from earlier commits
are found by the coordinator's scan, so no keyed state is needed. CDC mode
would require topics keyed this way, which is Debezium's default.

Bryan, Ryan, since you made the original call, I'd like to hear whether
this changes it for you.

[3] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/10842
[4] https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#row-lineage

Thanks,

Hi all,

This continues the collation work in #16972 [3]. We already aligned on
keeping multiple collation versions per file in [4]. The remaining question
is how to store the bounds.

Alex and I went through the options offline. I prototyped the two earlier
layouts in iceberg-go [1]. On real manifests they end up within ~2.5% of
each other after compression, so I don’t think size should drive the choice.

Ryan’s stats-only fields proposal [2] gives us a cleaner way to do this
without adding collation-specific fields to `content_stats`, which was
Russell’s main concern with the current PR.

The proposed shape is:

- Collation bounds are stored as a new stats-only field type. The field
points to the source column and records the collation + collation version.
Lower/upper bounds are original string values ordered by that collation.
They must be valid bounds, but do not need to be tight.
- `min_code_point(col)` and `max_code_point(col)` are separate `expr-value`
stats-only fields. They are ints and do not depend on collation version.
- A collated column therefore has 2 + N stats-only fields, where N is the
number of collation versions that have written stats. A file normally
carries bounds for only the version its writer used.
- If a writer uses a version that does not have a stats-only field yet, it
adds one through a table metadata update. No schema change.
- A reader uses bounds for its own version when present. It can also use
another version when the file’s code-point range has the same ordering in
both versions, for example some ASCII-only cases. Otherwise it just scans
the file.
- Readers without collation support ignore these fields like any other
unsupported stats-only field type.
- Old version fields can be removed later. That only means losing pruning
on files that still have stats for that version.

I don’t think plain `expr-value` is enough for the collation bounds
themselves. The bounds are ordered by the collation, not by the physical
type. Returning sort keys would make byte comparison work, but sort keys
can change across collation versions even when the relative order does not,
which would prevent reuse across versions.

Which code-point ranges keep their order across versions is up to the
engine. ICU does not publish this, so the format records the range and the
engine decides whether it can reuse a bound. An engine that cannot tell
scans the file.

I updated #16972 [3] to match this direction: no collation-specific
`content_stats`, one new stats-only field type for collation bounds, and
`min_code_point` / `max_code_point` in the functions appendix. It depends
on #18405.

Comments welcome here or on the PR.

and https://github.com/laskoviymishka/iceberg-go/tree/collation-size/derived

https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18405
[3] https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16972
[4] https://lists.apache.org/thread/4p8345gb8jo03l27qh86kbbpvolwc09j

Thanks,

Closing the loop on this thread: multi-version per file is settled.

written under the old one until they are rewritten. With several, a file
can carry bounds for each version, and bounds for a new version can be
added later.

Two weeks ago at Community Over Code in Glasgow, we held a brief
meeting to discuss authentication in the Iceberg REST client. Many
thanks to everyone who participated!

We agreed that there is a pressing need for improved OAuth2 support.
But unfortunately, progress on OAuth2Manager v2 has been slow, mostly
due to scope creep.

To unblock progress, we came up with two key initiatives:

dependency-free.

BearerAuthManager for its flexibility.

Hi everyone,

Here is a summary of yesterday's index sync. Thanks to everyone who joined.

1. Index spec (#16961 <https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16961>)
We went over the two questions Péter listed:
- Region file boundary: the per-column group max value is replaced by a
top-level max_ordering_key in each tracking file entry.
- Region file schema: the index now stores its own schema, with a mapping
from table fields to index fields, so index field IDs are independent of
the table's. Computed values are derived columns, either stored in the
region files (like a SQL generated column) or kept only as stats. This
depends on the derived columns proposal for V4, and the index keeps its
schema history (for example after int to long promotion).
There are no open issues left on the spec PR. Please review:
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16961

2. Index REST spec
Agreed:
- An index must be in the same namespace as its table. Cross-namespace
indexes are dropped.
- Rename and register are left out of the first version, to reduce
complexity. We can add them later if there is demand.

Main open question: should index routes be namespace-level (as in the PR),

Hi all,

I'd like to get some eyes on a PR that fixes a credentials mismatch in
remove_orphan_files, and agree on the approach before I port it across
Spark versions:

https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17862 (closes #17860)

Problem

Unless prefix_listing is enabled, DeleteOrphanFilesSparkAction lists the
table location with a Hadoop FileSystem built from the Spark session
configuration alone, while every other file operation in the action goes
through table.io(). When a catalog reaches its storage with credentials
other than the cluster's (e.g. a catalog that assumes a role in another AWS
account), reads and deletes succeed but the listing fails with AccessDenied
or silently sees no files.

Change

- DeleteOrphanFilesSparkAction gets a new catalogName(String) method. When
set, the listing uses the session Hadoop configuration plus that catalog's
spark.sql.catalog.<name>.hadoop.* overrides
(SparkUtil.hadoopConfCatalogOverrides). When not set, behavior is unchanged.
- RemoveOrphanFilesProcedure passes the catalog it was invoked on, so CALL
<catalog>.system.remove_orphan_files(...) picks up that catalog's overrides
with no new procedure argument.
- spark-procedures.md documents which configuration the listing uses.

The catalog is passed explicitly rather than inferred from Table.name(): as
@yangshangqing95 pointed out in review, a table name's first segment isn't
guaranteed to identify the Spark catalog it came from, and resolving it via
CatalogManager can initialize unrelated catalogs as a side effect.

Tests cover the procedure path across the test catalogs and the action API
with both SparkCatalog and SparkSessionCatalog, using a marker FileSystem
registered only in the catalog's hadoop.* overrides.

Questions

1. Is a catalogName(String) method on the action an acceptable public API
addition, or would people prefer a different shape?
2. The PR was opened against Spark 4.1 before the 4.2 module landed. If the
direction is agreed, I'll move the change to 4.2 and backport it to 4.1,
4.0 and 3.5.

Thanks,
Sebastian Daberdaku

body:
Hi everyone,

Following up on my action item from Monday's sync: here is what I found on
how databases, catalogs, and REST APIs model, list, and name indexes.

1. Where an index lives

   - Iceberg REST spec: resources that belong to one table are already
   nested under it, for example .../tables/{table}/plan, /credentials, and
   /metrics.
   - Catalog and REST APIs scope indexes to the table. None of them makes
   an index a top-level namespace object.
      - Lance (/v1/table/{id}/index/{index_name}) and Firestore put the
      index under the table in the URL path.
      - Glue (DatabaseName + TableName + IndexName) and Hive Metastore
      (get_indexes(db, tbl)) require the table to address an index.
   - SQL databases are split.
      - MySQL, SQL Server, Snowflake, and BigQuery make index names unique
      per table, so you name the table to address an index (for example DROP
      INDEX idx ON tbl in MySQL).
      - Postgres, Oracle, and SQLite make an index a schema object (DROP
      INDEX idx). Even Postgres always creates the index in its table's schema.

2. Listing across tables
Most SQL databases also list indexes across tables, separately from where
the index lives. For example, Snowflake has SHOW INDEXES IN SCHEMA /
DATABASE / ACCOUNT, and MySQL and Postgres have system views
(information_schema.STATISTICS and pg_indexes) that return every index in a
schema in one query. This covers the maintenance use case: find every index
in a namespace without going table by table.

3. Rename
MySQL, SQL Server, Postgres, and Oracle support index rename, mainly for
naming cleanup and schema migration tools. Glue, Lance, Firestore, and
BigQuery don't. That supports leaving it out of the first version.

Proposal:

   - Nest index routes under the table:
   /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}/indexes[/{index}]
   - Make index names unique per table. The index identifier then includes
   its table identifier plus the index name.
   - Add a second, optional endpoint that lists all indexes in a namespace,
   for maintenance: GET /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/indexes. For each
   index, it returns the index name and the table it belongs to. Catalogs
   don't have to support it.

Feedback welcome.

Thanks,
Huaxin

body:
Hi all,

I'm Michalis Papadimitriou from the TornadoVM team
https://github.com/beehive-lab/TornadoVM). TornadoVM compilesplain Java
methods into GPU kernels; latest is release 8.0.0 under Apache 2.0

We have built a proof of concept, iceberg-tornadovm: a library on Iceberg
1.12's public APIs that runs merge-on-read scans and table maintenance on
NVIDIA GPUs. Iceberg still plans and commits (planFiles, RewriteFiles,
RowDelta with their usual validations); the GPU only does the per-row work
in between. It needs no engine and no change to Iceberg.

What it covers today:
- Merge-on-read scans with position deletes, equality deletes and v3
  deletion vectors applied on the GPU
- Equality deletes -> deletion vectors (v3) or file-scoped position
  deletes (v2)
- Delete by key, written as deletion vectors
- NDV theta sketches into Puffin
- Compaction: bin-pack, sorted and Z-order

Every operation has a CPU version using the same algorithm, as a reference.

Early results (Spark 3.5.9, Iceberg 1.12):
- 3.9-4.8x faster merge-on-read scans at 5B rows (2x A10 vs 128 CPU
  threads), scaling ~2x from one GPU to two
- Equality-delete -> DV conversion 106x cheaper than Spark compaction
  (TPC-DS SF100: 0.77 s vs 81.9 s)
- 14x faster NDV statistics than compute_table_stats (2B rows)
- 1.8-8.6x faster compaction than Spark on CPU

We think that v4 decision to forbid new equality deletes (#17783),
converting
existing ones becomes a required work, which is where the GPU can help the
most.

We'd like to discuss the possibility of an upstream path , and would value
the
community's view on:
1. Home: should this stay out of tree, following the direction taken with
   Comet (#15674), or is there interest in a contrib/optional module?
2. Hooks: the FileFormat API (#12774) covers much of what we need. Are there
   other extension points (e.g. a pluggable rewrite-group runner or delete
   applier) the community would accept, so accelerators don't need forks?
3. Validation: which benchmarks or correctness suites would you want to see
   before discussing this further?

Any other input it would be great.
We're happy to share the code and  benchmark harness, or to present at a
community sync if that's useful.

Thanks,
Michalis Papadimitriou
TornadoVM team

Hi all,

I'd appreciate a review of https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18463.

GCSFileIO.deleteFiles currently can't tell a missing object from a failed
delete, because Storage.delete(Iterable<BlobId>) returns false for both.
Real failures, such as permission errors, are silently swallowed, so
callers have nothing to retry.

The PR switches deleteFiles to StorageBatch, which reports each object's
outcome separately.
- A missing object counts as success, so retries are safe to repeat.
- Any real failure is raised as BulkDeletionFailureException, so the caller
knows what failed and can retry it.
- If the batch request itself fails, every object in that batch is reported
as failed.

Regards,
Munendra S N

body:
Hi,

I propose adding a _last_updated_time metadata column to row lineage for v4
tables. It records the timestamp of the snapshot that last updated a row,
complementing _last_updated_sequence_number with a wall-clock time.

Summary of the spec change:
* New reserved metadata column _last_updated_time (timestamptz).
* New optional tracking field snapshot_timestamp (timestamptz) in v4
manifests.
  Writers leave it null for added entries and for entries modified by
  column files. On read, a null value is inherited from the snapshot's
  timestamp-ms.
* Upgrading to v4 does not require rewriting manifest lists or manifests.
  Pre-v4 metadata is read as if snapshot_timestamp is null, so exising rows
  get the timestamp of the last snapshot before the v4 upgrade.

This works well with the earlier v4 spec change that requires monotonically
increasing snapshot timestamps (#16294). Because each snapshot's
timestamp-ms
is strictly greater than its parent's on the same branch, _last_updated_time
follows the same order as _last_updated_sequence_number.

This enables queries for *when a row was last updated* and for
*rows modified **since a given time*, without mapping sequence numbers
back to snapshots that may have expired.

*Spec PR:* https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18526

Please vote in the next 72 hours:

[ ] +0 No preference
[ ] -1 Do not adopt the spec change (please explain)

Thanks, Steven

Hi all,

remove_orphan_files with a file_list_view filters the list with a raw
startsWith(location). For a location like s3://bucket/table, that also
matches s3://bucket/table-backup/..., so files in a sibling directory can
be treated as orphans and deleted (#16493). Russell called the filter
"worth fixing as a normal bug", and Ryan said it seems reasonable to fix it
in a separate PR.

#16498 matches on the location as a directory instead. This changes only
the file-list path, since directory listing is already bounded:
- entries under a sibling prefix such as table-backup are no longer in scope
- an entry equal to the location itself is no longer in scope

Anyone relying on a partial prefix, for example location =
s3://bucket/table to clean both table and table-backup, would need to run
the action once per directory. I don't expect that to be common, but it is
a behavior change, so Sung  asked to raise it here.

#18029 proposes the same check but keeps an entry equal to the location in
scope.

If there are no objections within a week, I'd like to go ahead with #16498
on Spark 4.2 and backport it to 3.5, 4.0 and 4.1 afterwards.

https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/16498
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/issues/16493
